# doj-kim-letter-2026-06-17
- **URL:** https://fingfx.thomsonreuters.com/gfx/legaldocs/xmpjxkkompr/DOJ%20response%20Kim%20quash%20OpenAI%20records%202026.pdf · **Accessed:** 2026-09-16 (7 pp., read in full via a reader proxy) · **For:** v1 response round, item 7
- **What it establishes:** United States v. Richard Kim, 25 Cr. 359 (LGS) (S.D.N.Y.), Dkt. 55, Government letter of June 17, 2026 (AUSAs Ryan T. Nees and Michael DiBattista; U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton) opposing Kim's June 15 motion to quash. Facts: two § 2703 warrants for "seven accounts held by the defendant at two artificial intelligence ('AI') companies, Anthropic PBC and OpenAI OpCo, LLC," issued by Magistrate Judge Robert W. Lehrburger on May 21, 2026, served the same day, 14-day return; device searches had already yielded "numerous prompts Kim submitted to ChatGPT," notes about his use of Claude and ChatGPT, subscription banking records, and subscriber records across pseudonymous emails; Kim had wiped devices after fleeing to South Korea in July 2024. Law: the SCA lets only providers move to quash, in two narrow circumstances; § 2708 makes SCA remedies exclusive; the remedy is post-execution suppression (Grubbs; Google LLC v. United States, D.D.C. 2025). Privilege: cites Heppner, 820 F. Supp. 3d 292, 296–97; filter teams handle any privilege. Kim's motion challenged only the OpenAI warrant (n. 3).
- **Key passages:** p. 2: "The SCA provides no authority for criminal defendants, such as Kim, to quash or modify a search warrant issued pursuant to a provider." / p. 3: "the proper remedy for the defendant's claims is a motion to suppress, not a motion to quash, and the SCA authorizes service providers, not users, to move to quash". / p. 6: "users of AI tools (particularly trained lawyers like the defendant) can have no reasonable expectation of confidentiality in their communications with chatbots (which user queries and responses are used by AI companies to continuously learn and develop the chatbots)". / p. 4: the affidavit foresaw Kim "researching methods of concealing evidence, laundering proceeds, or even discussing with chatbots his purported gambling addiction".
- **Reliability:** Primary (court filing by a party); adversarial, but the procedural facts (dates, accounts, magistrate) are reliable.
- **Relevance to this project:** Item 7; establishes that both major providers received warrants for one defendant's accounts and the government's position that users have no pre-execution remedy.
- **Slice L addendum (re-opened 2026-09-16, v2→v3 response round):** Re-read locally for the Heppner reporter cite, verbatim at p. 6: "See United States v. Heppner, 820 F. Supp. 3d 292, 296–97 (S.D.N.Y. 2026)" and "See Heppner, 820 F. Supp. 3d at 298." This is the only place I have seen the F. Supp. 3d citation; it is a party's filing, so verify against Westlaw/Lexis before printing pin cites.
